The DPA found that the CCTV installed for the purpose of crime prevention didn’t automatically exempted a data subject from having access to their data.

Avanza Bank notified IMY of a personal data incident: between 15 November 2019 and 2 June 2021 the Meta pixel's Automatic Advanced Matching and Automatic Events functions, activated by mistake, sent data of roughly 500,000 to 1 million people to Meta, including personal identity numbers, loan amounts and account numbers. Much of it was sent in plain text from logged-in areas. IMY found the bank lacked appropriate security measures, did not follow its own routines and could not detect the transfer, breaching Articles 32(1) and 5(1)(f) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 15,000,000, assessing the seriousness as low within the range for Article 5(1)(f) infringements.

A patient complained that a surgeon never answered her access request for the pre-operative photographs taken before her operation. The surgeon only supplied them 302 days later, after the Garante invited him to comply. The Garante also found that the retention period in his privacy notice was too generic. It declared the processing unlawful, fined him EUR 4,000, ordered him to rewrite the notice within 40 days and ordered publication of the decision. The case against the healthcare facility was closed.

A complainant objected that a ranking list from a preselection test of a public competition, naming admitted and non-admitted candidates, stayed online and indexed by search engines on the Municipality of Nepi's website despite removal requests. The Garante found the list was published from 3 February 2015 to 18 February 2022 without a legal basis. It also found the Municipality had no Article 28 data processing agreement with its web management provider until November 2022. It fined the Municipality EUR 8,000 for the publication and EUR 12,000 for the missing processor agreement, EUR 20,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee complained that his employer, TS Food Processing, had not answered his access request for personal data stored on the company PC he used. The company first refused, citing fear of trade secrets being taken, then said the request was too generic. Access was given only after the Garante opened its investigation, about two years late. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR, fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian Garante examined two proceedings against telecom operator Fastweb, started after many complaints and reports about unwanted promotional calls, use of customer contact data for marketing, weak information notices and late replies to data subject requests. It found that Fastweb failed to check the Public Opposition Register for numbers called after web-sales consent, relied on legitimate interest instead of consent for marketing to customers (including up to 24 months after contract end), gave unclear privacy notices and did not answer rights requests on time. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000,000 and several corrective orders, including a ban on processing numbers whose marketing consent was collected via websales, a double opt-in system and a rewritten notice and consent form. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA learned from public sources that the municipality of Forlì offered the 'Falco – Città protetta' app, letting citizens send reports to the local police, who could check CCTV images and collect the reporter's GPS position and phone number. After an investigation it found unlawful processing both in the video surveillance systems and in the Falco app, including failures on transparency, privacy by design, processor contract, security and the DPIA. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 for the video surveillance violations and EUR 5,000 for the Falco violations, EUR 15,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended.

The DPA reprimanded a municipality for disclosing a Member of Parliament’s personal data after she publicly complained about speeding fines. The DPA held that the municipality had no legal basis to disclose the data even if the information was already publicly available.
The DPA reprimanded a bus operator for publishing the personal phone numbers of its employees on the company intranet for other employees to access.
The DPA found the controller was in breach of Article 12 GDPR and Article 15 GDPR because it didn’t answer access request within one-month period.

The DPA decided to close the case on unlawful processing of a business e-mail address data, referring to the DPA's expediency requirement. According to the DPA, the case encompassed a broader dispute, not to be solved by the DPA decision.

The DPA declared the controller violated Article 12 GDPR and Article 17 GDPR by failing to answer erasure request in timely manner. No corrective measures were imposed as the controller remedied the breach, deleting the data during the investigation.

A public healthcare facility reported a ransomware attack of 10 February 2022 that encrypted its servers holding data of about 30,000 patients and over 1,100 staff, including health data. The Polish DPA found that the facility had not carried out a risk analysis, had not adequately tested its security measures, and had not notified the data subjects of the breach. It imposed a fine of PLN 40,000 and ordered the facility to notify the affected people within 30 days and to bring its security measures into line within 90 days after a risk analysis. The infringement of security was found to be negligent, while the failure to notify was a conscious decision.
The DPA found that a school can partially refuse to act on an access request filed by the parent of a data subject, if the disclosure of certain data can impair the best interest of the minor.

The DPA found that a bank violated the principle of accuracy when it transferred incorrect information about a data subject’s address to an insolvency registry, preventing the latter from notifying the data subject that a processing occurred. The bank paid a reduced fine of €120,000 in accordance with national law.

An individual (controller) was fined €10,000 for unlawfully publishing the names, addresses, telephone numbers, data concerning health and images of ten data subject on Telegram and YouTube with the aim of encouraging others to make abusive phone calls.

The DPA dismissed a complaint against a newspaper, finding that it was publishing information in the public interest and was thus exempt under national law from certain GDPR provisions. It noted that the exemption applies where there is a close nexus between the personal data published and the public interest - including where special categories of data are involved.

The DPA reprimanded a media company for a failure to provide the data subject, a politician, with the information listed in Articles 13 and 14 GDPR. On the other hand, the DPA found that using a drone to take pictures of the data subject's house was lawful under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR.
The DPA held that, in light of recent CJEU case law, the Ministry of Interior and Health must provide the data subject with information about the security logs of the civil registration system.

An employee of a car dealership complained about two workplace systems: a facial recognition time-attendance device and a workshop management software that logged each mechanic's work and pauses. After an inspection by the Guardia di Finanza, the Garante found that biometric processing of employees had no valid legal basis, was disproportionate, kept biometric data until employment ended, and relied on an inadequate privacy notice. The management software was also used without a valid legal basis or adequate information. The Garante fined the company EUR 120,000, banned the biometric processing, and ordered the company to bring the software processing into compliance within 90 days.

The Garante investigated Eni Plenitude after 108 reports and 7 complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls made without consent or to numbers listed in the Public Opposition Register. It found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, accuracy and security, telemarketing without a valid legal basis, and failure to put in place security measures and monitoring over the whole sales chain. It imposed a fine of EUR 6,419,631 (2% of the maximum), a ban on further processing of the complainants' data, and orders to inform 657 data subjects and strengthen controls. The decision is also published.

A woman complained that a car rental company refused her a rental voucher because she was on a 'black list'. The investigation showed that the company's parent bank queried the public SCIPAFI identity-fraud system on its behalf, without Ministry authorisation, and passed the result to the rental company through an internal watchlist. The Garante found the processing unlawful, and also found that the data processing agreement between the bank and the rental company did not make the bank a valid processor. It fined the bank EUR 1,000,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The operative part cites Articles 12(3) and 15, while the reasoning deals with Articles 5(1)(a) and 28.

A local health authority answered a prison administration's request to verify a disability certificate by sending a full copy of the medical commission report. The back of the sheet showed the complainant's medical history in clear, including HIV infection. The authority blamed an operator's material error during a COVID staffing shortage. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching data minimisation, integrity/confidentiality and security obligations, and Article 75 of the Italian Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 24,000 and ordered publication, with no corrective orders since the conduct had ceased.

The DPA fined a bank €1,000,000 after it unlawfully accessed a government database for fraud prevention. The bank used its own access permission in order to access the database on behalf of another company from the same corporate group.

The DPA held that a controller cannot systematically require data subjects to deliver a signed form to the controller's premises in order to exercise the right of access, as facilitating the data subject's rights under the GDPR requires a case-by-case assessment.
The DPA fined a controller €6,000 for ignoring erasure requests that were not sent to the controller’s designated email address provided in their privacy policy.

A customer asked the company to erase his data and stopped receiving marketing, but the company kept sending promotional emails for months and never answered his erasure and objection requests, even after the complaint was filed. The Litigation Chamber found negligence, noting the company still had not replied by the hearing date. It imposed an administrative fine, starting from an EDPB-guideline-based amount of EUR 245,000 and reducing it by about 30% to EUR 172,431 because of the company's financial situation.

The DPA confirmed its previous fine of €70,000 on a bank, finding that it lacked a legal basis to process personal data that was stolen and that the controller was negligent in verifying the identity of the data subject for a credit application.
The DPA fined a controller €300 for using a video surveillance camera for home security which captured a neighbor’s patio.
The APD issued a reprimand against a controller for responding orally to an access request and for not providing the information regarding the processing due to its apparent obviousness.

Hundreds of Greeks abroad registered on the special overseas electoral rolls complained after receiving unsolicited political e-mails from an MEP on the e-mail addresses they had given to the Ministry of Interior's platform. The Authority investigated both the MEP and the Ministry. The decision is a single text with two separate parts. Against the MEP, it found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) with Articles 6(1) and 14 GDPR, fined her EUR 40,000 and ordered deletion of the data. For the Ministry of Interior, it found breaches of the security, confidentiality, data protection by design, breach notification and records-of-processing provisions. It fined the Ministry EUR 400,000 and ordered it to document and review its data protection policies and measures, set a timetable, run audits and train staff. A decision on a political party and another individual was postponed.

Hundreds of Greeks living abroad complained that an MEP sent them an unsolicited political e-mail at the personal address they had given to register on the special overseas electoral rolls through the Ministry of Interior platform. The Authority found that the MEP processed overseas voters' e-mail addresses without a valid legal basis and without informing them, breaching the principle of lawfulness, objectivity and transparency (Art. 5(1)(a)), Art. 6(1) and Art. 14 GDPR. It fined the MEP EUR 40,000 and ordered her to erase all the overseas voters' data. In the same decision it fined the Ministry of Interior EUR 400,000 for security and accountability failings, and it postponed the decision on a political party and another person.

The DPA imposed €400,000 and €40,000 fine on the Ministry of Interior and an MEP, respectively, for unsolicited political communication to data subjects' email addresses, which were provided to the MEP by the Ministry of the Interior.

A patient asked the Rhodense health authority to correct his residence and health-domicile addresses, sending the request to its general institutional certified email. The authority did not answer for 156 days and corrected the data only after he complained to the Garante. The Garante held that the general institutional address was not a 'random or incorrect' address under the EDPB access guidelines, so the request had to be handled within the Article 12 deadlines. It found breaches of the accuracy principle and of Articles 12 and 16, and imposed a fine of EUR 4,500 plus publication of the decision. No corrective orders were needed because the conduct had ended.

A secretary of a neurology outpatient clinic of the local health authority ASL TO4 emailed a circular on therapeutic plans to 45 multiple sclerosis patients, with all addresses visible in the CC field, and then sent a correction the same way. This disclosed the patients' health status to each other. The authority notified the breach and the Garante found a violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It rejected the defence of excusable human error. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,400 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective orders since the conduct had ceased and measures were being implemented.

A tenant filed a complaint against a technician who processed his landlord’s personal data. The DPA rejected the complaint since the tenant was neither a data subject nor was affected by the data processing.
The DPA held that the use of video surveillance to justify the dismissal of an employee violates the purpose limitation principle if it was initially installed to ensure the safety of employees.
The DPA fined a municipality €3,000 for using records from video-surveillance systems in disciplinary proceedings against employees in lack of trade union agreements or public authorisation.

The Polish data protection authority found that a medical services company had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures. It had no proper risk analysis, outdated system software on edge devices, configuration errors and no procedures for regularly testing security measures. The case began with the company's own breach notification and an inspection. The authority ordered the company to fix its processing within 30 days and imposed an administrative fine of PLN 1,440,549, equal to EUR 330,000, using the EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 method.
The DPA held that the use of a data subject’s email address for political advertising purposes must be based on consent.

Following a ransomware attack involving data from the Federal Government, the Federal Data Protection and Transparency Officer reprimanded a software provider for its lack of appropriate measures to ensure data protection.

The Dutch DPA fined Clearview AI Inc., a US company offering facial recognition services built on billions of photos scraped from the internet, a total of EUR 30.5 million. It found unlawful processing of personal data and biometric data of people in the Netherlands, insufficient information to data subjects, failure to answer two access requests and failure to facilitate access rights. The missing EU representative (Art. 27) was also an infringement, but no fine was imposed for it because the Italian and Greek authorities had already fined it. The AP also imposed four periodic penalty payments to force Clearview to end the continuing infringements. Clearview refused to provide turnover information, so the AP used the EUR 20 million maximum as the basis.

The DPA issued a reprimand to the Birmingham Children’s Trust Community Interest Company for a data breach related to the production of a child care protection plan that included inappropriate personal data in the form of criminal allegations against a child.

The DPA considered that its intervention in a case regarding the installation of surveillance cameras in the common areas of a co-owned building was not strictly necessary, as it was an ancillary to a broader dispute. Therefore, the DPA dismissed the case.

A man complained that he received a promotional email from a hotel company he had never dealt with, and that his access request went unanswered. The company could not show consent or where it got his data, gave contradictory answers to the Garante, and deleted his data after the investigation began. The Garante found breaches of the consent rules for marketing and of the right of access, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the order.

The Garante examined four breach notifications and one complaint about improper access to patients' electronic health dossiers at the Padua university hospital. Health staff looked at records of patients they were no longer treating, to review outcomes of earlier cases. In other cases unknown persons used the credentials of staff who left workstations open, and an administrative employee accessed a patient-employee's dossier without any care purpose. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), (c), (f), 9, 25 and 32 GDPR. It imposed three fines of EUR 25,000 each (EUR 75,000 in total), ordered the hospital to remove two access reasons from the system, requested further information and ordered publication.
The document is an opinion of the Data Protection Authority on the draft regulation for digital infrastructure and cloud services for public administration.

The DPA issued a reprimand against a hospital. It held that data about the symptoms of an employee who is on sick leave are health data and forwarding such data to the hospital’s general director is unnecessary for the purposes of finding a replacement for the employee.

The Italian Data Protection Authority held a meeting on May 9, 2024, involving key members, to address a significant data breach incident affecting the "Ordine degli Avvocati di Roma" and managed by InfoCert S.p.a.
The DPA fined Vodafone Spain €200,000 for failing to implement safeguards which would have prevented the unauthorised delivery of a sim card to a third party.

The Romanian authority's press release reports two investigations opened after personal data breach notifications. For Centrul Medical Unirea SRL, personal data of many patients and employees were disclosed on the internet without authorisation. The authority found inadequate technical and organisational security measures and fined the company RON 24,856 (about EUR 5,000), also ordering a review and update of its measures. A second operator, Genpact România SRL, was fined separately, which is outside this record.
The DPA reprimanded the City of Copenhagen for failing to prevent potential access to personal data of 3.7 million people by unauthorised 37,500 employees.

4Finance Spain (VIVUS) notified the AEPD of a personal data breach in which attackers used valid customer credentials to log into customer web areas and take out fraudulent loans, affecting about 9,500 customers. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings for breach of Art. 5(1)(f) (proposed fine EUR 200,000) and Art. 32 GDPR (proposed fine EUR 400,000), a total of EUR 600,000. The company paid EUR 360,000 on 25 April 2024, applying both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and voluntary payment). The AEPD therefore declared the proceedings terminated under Art. 85 LPACAP.
In a prima facie decision the DPA ordered the provider of a weekly magazine to comply with a data subject’s access request within one month.

The DPA issued a warning against a controller for not implementing transparent modalities regarding the closure of former employees’ mailboxes, specifically the retention period of the mailbox. The controller has one month to proceed to the deletion of the email address and mailbox, period which can be extended to three months with the data subject's consent.

The DPA found that a controller violated the principles of accuracy and data minimization by characterising a document as a “duplicate” and submitting it to a court even though the document contained a modified and inaccurate address of a data subject.

The DPA reprimanded a telecom operator for storing customer data for more than three years after the end of the customer relationship, which was considered the maximum justified period of time to defend itself against possible invoicing claims.
The DPA dismissed a complaint filed by a data subject after a data breach. It found the controller’s technical and organisational measures under Article 32 GDPR were appropriate.

The Dutch DPA investigated the cookie practices of kruidvat.nl, operated by A.S. Watson, after a 2019 sweep and a warning letter that did not lead to changes. It found that tracking cookies were placed without valid consent between 28 April 2020 and 1 October 2020, so there was no lawful basis for the processing. The AP imposed a fine of EUR 600,000 under category III of its fining policy, taking the group's turnover into account and treating the long delay since the investigation report as mitigating. The company has lodged an objection against the decision.

The DPA held that a municipality processing a third party’s criminal data to adequately justify a marriage refusal decision was disproportionate and could have been attained by less intrusive measures, for example anonymisation of the data.

The DPA imposed a €8,730 (£7,500) fine on the YMCA for violating UK GDPR security obligations by sending an email directed to HIV-positive individuals using CC instead of BCC, and noted that the use of BCC was a high-risk practice due to human error.

The DPA fined a postal service €12,680 (HUF 5 million) for adding unsolicited content to its delivery updates. While a customer satisfaction questionnaire did not require a separate legal basis, the inclusion of direct marketing information did.
The DPA fined a company €54,600 after the loss of a flash drive containing unencrypted employee data led to a data breach.

As part of the EDPB coordinated action on data protection officers, the Greek authority sent a questionnaire to 31 public bodies, including the Ministry of Climate Crisis and Civil Protection. The Ministry did not answer on time, even after a reminder, and had not designated a DPO or published or notified DPO contact details since its creation. It also had not complied with GDPR chapters 3 and 4 (transparency, data protection by design and default, records of processing, security). The Authority found violations of Articles 31, 37, 12, 32, 25, 30 and 5(1)(a), (c), (f), and imposed three fines totalling EUR 50,000. The Ministry's arguments about being newly created and lacking resources were rejected.

The DPA found that the administrator of a software platform allowing people to book doctor's appointments was a processor as it did not determine the purposes of the processing, and did therefore not have to respond to an access request. The purposes were determined by the health care institutions.

The text is the CNIL's overview page of sanctions issued by its restricted committee, not the decision itself. One row dated 25/04/2024 concerns an association participating in the activities of political organisations, handled under the simplified procedure. The listed shortcoming is lack of a legal basis, and the sanction is an administrative fine of EUR 16,000 plus an injunction. No reasoning, articles or facts of the case are given.

The local police reported a shop run by Dly S.r.l. in a shopping centre, and the Guardia di finanza inspected it on 5 July 2023. It found six working cameras that filmed customers and employees, viewable live and recorded on the owners' private smartphones. The system was installed without a union agreement or Labour Inspectorate authorisation, as Article 4 of Law 300/1970 requires. An authorisation from 2019 for a different shop did not count. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned it until the safeguards are in place, and fined the company EUR 5,000.

A temporary agency worker placed with the company complained that it did not give him copies of his training certificates after his access request. The company said it had deleted the certificates after the employment ended and did not state reasons for refusal or mention the right to complain. Only after the Garante opened the investigation did it obtain and send some certificates, almost eleven months later. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in relation to Article 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

A former employee of GSE complained that the company never answered his access requests of October and December 2021 for his performance evaluation files for 2019 and 2020. The company only supplied the documents in September 2022, about eleven months after the first request and after learning of the complaint to the Garante. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR, rejected the excuse of an IT mishap and the argument that the employee already knew the content. It fined the company EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant received unsolicited promotional emails from an e-commerce paper company, then dozens of anomalous emails, and got no reply to his rights request, which the company said ended up in spam. The Garante's technical checks showed the company's website ran an obsolete PrestaShop CMS with known serious vulnerabilities, even after the authority contacted it. It found violations of security and accountability duties, of data subject rights and of the lawful basis and consent rules for marketing. It ordered the company to update its security measures and pay a EUR 30,000 fine. The missing breach notification was treated as absorbed in the security violation.

The DPA issued a warning against the Ministry of Justice for processing personal data uploaded on a dating website by an employee. Although data was processed in the context of disciplinary proceedings, the controller did not have a legal basis.

The DPA fined a controller €279,100 (GBP 240,000) for making direct marketing calls to data subjects on a ‘do not call’ register, noting that controllers must verify whether data subjects are on the register and cannot rely on data suppliers' assurances.

The DPA held that the controller failed to comply with the transparency principle by requesting an ID document as a deposit when renting a mobility aid, whilst failing to present an existing alternative to the data subject.

Clyde Valley Housing Association have received a reprimand from the commissioner because of an infringement that occurred in July 2022 when they released a new customer portal with data subjects personal information visible to all other residents.

The DPA instructed Google to comply with an erasure request by immediately removing specific search results linked to the complainant's name and deleting any similar links appearing in the search engine.

The Czech data protection authority announced that Avast Software s.r.o. was finally fined CZK 351 million for unlawful processing of personal data of users of its antivirus software and browser extensions. In part of 2019 Avast passed pseudonymised browsing history linked to a unique identifier, covering about 100 million users, to Jumpshot, INC. Users were wrongly told the data was anonymous and used for trend analysis; the proceedings showed the data was not anonymised and could re-identify at least some people. The case was handled with other EU supervisory authorities under the One Stop Shop mechanism. This is a press release, not the decision itself, so no articles are cited.

The DPA dismissed a complaint against a diagnostic centre, finding that the data subject's claims that the controller disclosed medical testing results to a family member without her consent were unsupported by the evidence presented.

The DPA fined a bank €2,000,000 for improperly obtaining data subjects' consent to process their personal data. The controller acknowledged its fault and paid a reduced fine of €1,200,000 in accordance with national law.

The Rome Chamber of Commerce notified a personal data breach: an SQL injection attack on the CMS of its website let attackers reach a backup copy of the online appointment system database, which was then published online. About 22,300 users' identity, contact and login data were exposed. The Garante found that Innova Camera, the Chamber's processor, had kept the old backup far longer than needed and had stored passwords with the weak MD5 hash. It fined Innova Camera EUR 25,000 in total (EUR 10,000 for storage limitation and EUR 15,000 for integrity/confidentiality and security), and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because remedial measures had already been taken.

The Italian DPA checked the website of the Libero Consorzio comunale di Enna and found no DPO contact details and no notification of them to the Authority. The investigation showed the DPO was designated more than three and a half years after the GDPR applied, contact details were published and communicated late, and the DPO was an employee running several services, lacking time and exposed to conflicts of interest. The Garante found violations of Articles 37(1) and (7) and 38(2) and (6) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 6,000, plus publication of the decision.

The Garante investigated an energy supplier after 56 reports and 2 complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls that led to unrequested energy contract activations. A check with the Public Opposition Register showed 106 numbers in a sample week had been called while registered. The Garante found failures of accountability, lawful basis, security and control over the sales chain and partners, and breach of Art. 130 of the Code. It banned further processing of the complainants' data, ordered notification to the 106 people and better controls over the sales network, and fined the company EUR 100,000, also ordering publication.

A candidate in a public competition for 1858 social protection posts complained that INPS had published on its website lists of admitted and non-admitted candidates and the title evaluation with scores for each candidate. The Garante found that data of over 5,000 candidates were published and indexed by search engines without a suitable legal basis, since only final rankings of winners may be published, not intermediate results. It found breaches of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Code, and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 plus publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered as the lists had already been removed.

Cybersecurity and antivirus company Avast was fined €13.7 million - the highest fine ever imposed by the Czech DPA. The company failed to anonymize browsing data of more than 100 million users before sharing it with third parties for market analysis purposes.

The DPA fined a football club €200,000 for lacking a legal basis to process fingerprint data and violating obligations of necessity and proportionality. The controller acknowledged its fault and paid a reduced fine of €120,000 in accordance with national law.
The DPA prohibited the provider of a platform comparing church personnel from publishing a list of church personnel which received a questionnaire about their religious beliefs.

The DPA imposed €525,000 to HUBSIDE.STORE for carrying out canvassing campaigns using personal data obtained via forms that were deceptive by design and did not allow the controller to collect valid consent.

The DPA found a controller rightfully declined an erasure request in accordance with Article 17(3)(e) GDPR since the controller demonstrated that the data is needed for future criminal proceedings against the data subject.
The DPA considered that the possibility that personal data could contribute as evidence in a legal action in the future justifies the refusal to comply with an erasure request.
The DPA issued a warning against an embassy for, among other things, not giving access to the identity of an employee who made an unauthorized consultation of the data subject’s personal data.
The DPA fined a controller €1,000 after it failed to comply with a previous decision ordering it to remove a data subject’s unfavourable picture from its website.
The DPA issued a reprimand to a company as one of its employees negligently disclosed borrowers' financial information to their employers.

The DPA imposed a temporary ban on the Worldcoin Foundation's processing of biometric data, finding that it provided insufficient information for data subjects to consent, made it impossible to erase collected data or revoke consent, and collected large amounts of minors' sensitive data.

The DPA dismissed an appeal concerning an erasure request, finding that the controller made every necessary effort to delete images of the data subject from its social media, but was unable to delete all of the requested data as it awaited Meta's response.

The Catalan DPA fined FUOC €31,000 for violating Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by publishing a student’s project with excessive, non-anonymized data of 54 minors in its open-access repository, breaching the data minimisation principle.

A ransomware attack on the data centre run by LAZIOcrea, processor for the Lazio Region and several regional health bodies, made information systems of the local health authority Roma 3 unavailable, including systems holding patients' health data. The authority did not notify the breach to the Garante and did not document its reasoning or risk assessment for not notifying. The Garante found a violation of Article 33 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, rating the gravity as low. It took into account full cooperation, the Covid-19 emergency, late and partial information from the processor, and no previous infringements. The decision is to be published in full.

A ransomware attack hit the data centre run by LAZIOcrea, the in-house IT company of the Lazio Region, which was both controller for its own processing and processor for the Region, the Regional Council and several health service bodies. The Garante found that LAZIOcrea notified the breach late and incompletely as controller, notified the other controllers two weeks late as processor, and had inadequate security measures in both roles. It set four separate fines (16,000, 25,000, 90,000 and 140,000 euro) totalling 271,000 euro and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because remedial measures had already been taken.

The DPA issued a warning against the Worldcoin Foundation, finding that its processing of biometric data probably lacked a legal basis under the GDPR and would likely fail to meet standards of consent, due in part to the promise of free tokens in exchange for consent.

The DPA issued an enforcement notice to the Home Office, ordering it to bring its processing of personal data via GPS monitoring of migrants arriving in the UK into compliance with the UK GDPR after it failed to conduct an adequate data protection impact assessment.
The DPA considered that it is not competent to deal with a complaint regarding the right to erasure of data processed by the press in the exercise of its freedom of expression.
A residents association was fined €2,000 for posting a list of debtors in the building lobby and sharing it via email, in violation of the principle of confidentiality.
The DPA closed a case considering, among other things, that the complaint was manifestly excessive as it was filed almost 2 years and 9 months after the events took place.

The DPA imposed a fine of €1,720,425.16 (NOK 20,000,000) on the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration because it made special categories of personal data of a large number of people available for a long time without the necessary security mechanisms being established.

The Spanish DPA dismissed an internal appeal regarding a cookie banner decision, stating that the Spanish LSSI instead of the GDPR applies and that it would need to verify the data subject's claim which was not possible because the website was deactivated in the meanwhile.

The DPA rejected a complaint concerning the processing of personal data for the purpose of building and training a model which offered personalised discounts, noting that this practice could be understood as a legitimate interest of the controller.

The DPA imposed a €330,000 (PLN 1,440,549) to a bank for failing to notify the DPA and data subjects of a data breach concerning banking documents which contained numerous personal data, including names and national identification numbers.
The DPA imposed a fine of €18,000 (PLN 78,575) on Toyota Bank for a failure to adequately assess the risk of a data breach and for not notifying the DPA as required by Article 33 GDPR.
The DPA imposed a fine of €10,059.92 (ISK 1,500,00) on Stjörnuna ehf, the operator of Subway in Iceland, for unlawfully monitoring its employees without adequately informing them.
The DPA found a hospital to have breached the principle of data minimisation by including unique and virtually permanent identification numbers in text messages sent to patients.
The DPA found that Groupon lacked a legal basis for requiring a data subject’s ID in order to fulfill access and erasure requests, and thus violated data minimisation obligations.

The DPA found that Apple could retain a data subject's hashed email address as a security measure after receiving an erasure request. However, the DPA found Apple did not inform the data subject about such processing in violation of Article 13 GDPR.

A former bank employee complained that the bank gave only a partial reply to her access request for the data in her personnel file and in the disciplinary proceeding file. The bank sent the remaining documents (correspondence with a third party) only after the Garante intervened, and never told her why they had been withheld. The Garante rejected the bank's arguments, including that the access request served a different purpose, and found breaches of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 15 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Two former employees (one a former chairman of the board) complained that the company kept their individual work email accounts active for months after they left and accessed the messages, and that it gave no proper information about this. The Garante found that the company kept the accounts active until 16 November 2021 and its legal representative accessed their content without a lawful basis, instead of deactivating them with an automatic reply. It also found the privacy notice did not cover this processing. The Garante found breaches of Article 5(1)(a), (c), (e) and Article 13 GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 20,000, ordered publication, and asked the company to report on an automatic account-deactivation system and Article 13 compliance within 90 days.
The DPA decided that both responsible person of a legal entity and the legal entity are held liable for processing of personal data of former employees without their consent.

The DPA fined an IT retailer €856,000 for failing to determine the storage period of its customer data. The DPA also considered that the processing of personal data related to a single online purchase does not require the creation of a customer account.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation in February 2024 into a self-storage company that had notified a personal data breach after a cyber attack. The attack compromised the confidentiality and availability of customer data on its server, and the business was down for several weeks. The authority found that the company had not put appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place. It fined the company RON 24,884.50 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to implement access monitoring and logging with at least 30 days of log retention, backed up.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for sending direct marketing offers without an option to opt-out while claiming during the investigation, that the processing in question was suspended.
ICO has issued a reprimand to West Midlands Police after the force repeatedly mixed up two data subject's personal information, violating several articles of the UK Data Protection Act.

The DPA ordered Google to deindex some URLs relating to data subject's non-payment of employee salary and insurance. The DPA postponed the decision for 7 more URLs until the data subject presents the required additional evidence and court decisions.

The DPA ordered Google to deindex some URLs relating to the criminal conviction of a data subject's relative, which appeared as search results when the full name of the data subject was typed. However, it did not require Google to delete third party blog posts on a blog platform that it hosted.
The DPA issued a reprimand to the Cyprus News Agency for unlawfully transferring personal data to the U.S. via the use of Google Analytics without any legal basis
In one of the 101 complaints filed by noyb, the DPA reprimanded a private news company for transferring personal data in the US without a legal basis in accordance with Chapter V GDPR.

ELTA, the Greek postal operator, notified the authority of a ransomware attack in March 2022 that encrypted systems and led to personal data being leaked on the dark web. The authority investigated and found that ELTA had not kept adequate technical and organisational security measures, breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle and the security of processing obligation. It treated these as two separate infringements of high gravity affecting 4–5 million people. Taking into account aggravating and mitigating factors and ELTA's turnover, it imposed a fine of EUR 2,995,140, equal to 1% of the last annual turnover.

The DPA imposed a fine of total €168,709 on a Greek electric power supplier and its three affiliated companies for Unsolicited communications a violations of Article 11(1) Greek Law 3471/2006 and for inadequate security of processing Article 32 GDPR.

The Croatian DPA checked a company's website on its own initiative using the EDPS Website Evidence Collector and found that cookies, including analytics and marketing cookies, were set on first page load without informed consent. The cookie banner and privacy notice also did not give adequate information on legal basis, cookie types, purposes and retention. The Agency found breaches of Articles 6(1)(a), 7, 5(1)(a) and 13(1)-(2) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000, about 0.1% of the maximum possible fine, and ordered proof of payment. The company had introduced a new consent banner (Cookiebot in November 2022, Didomi in May 2023) during the proceedings.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for failing to honor the data subject's right to object to receiving payment reminders, even though the data subject consistently made timely payments.

The DPA confirmed that telecommunication service providers have to provide access to location data they process under national data retention legislation contrary to the controller who argued that such legislation provided a full exemption for the right to access.
The DPA ordered a controller who sent unsolicited letters to a data subject to erase their data after the latter had made an erasure request, to which the controller failed to respond.
The DPA fined a website provider €90,000 for setting unnecessary cookies without users’ consent and for not informing them about the existence and function of these cookies.

The DPA considered that an e-reputation consultancy company cannot represent a data subject under Article 80(1) GDPR, as it is for-profit body whose statutory objectives are not in the public interest.

A report to the Garante complained that the public transport company TPER used a season-ticket application form where consent to customer surveys/marketing and to service SMS looked mandatory and was not specific, with only a signature at the bottom. After investigating, the Garante found unlawful processing: invalid consent, deficient and unclear information notice, excessive 10-year retention, and failure to update documents by 25 May 2018 (accountability). It fined the company EUR 50,000, ordered a ban on using data collected on invalid consents for marketing and service communications, deletion of that data, and delivery of the new privacy notice to data subjects. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

A customer of the CoopVoce mobile service objected to promotional processing and asked for access to and erasure of his data, but the company did not properly handle the requests and kept sending promotional SMS. The Garante also inspected the company in April 2023 and found issues with consent wording for marketing, and with five-year retention of images collected at events and on social media. It found violations of the storage limitation principle, the 30-day deadline for replying to requests, the right of access, the right to object to marketing, and Article 130 of the Code. It ordered the company to change its marketing consent wording, and fined it EUR 90,000, with publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA received two complaints and two breach notifications about the South Tyrol health authority's corporate electronic health record (dossier sanitario), which health staff not involved in the patients' care had repeatedly accessed. The cases were merged. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching the basic principles, security and privacy-by-design rules, and special-category data rules. It imposed three fines of EUR 25,000 each, totalling EUR 75,000, and ordered publication. No corrective measures were imposed because the authority had started disciplinary proceedings and adapted its systems.

Sigma s.r.l., a Vodafone dealer with two shops in Trento province, was investigated by the Guardia di finanza. Its owners and staff activated SIM cards and services in customers' names without their knowledge and charged them for phones never delivered, using customer data and ID documents. The Garante found breaches of lawfulness, fairness, accountability, legal basis, data protection by design and information duties. It fined the company EUR 150,000, banned further processing of this kind, and ordered publication of the decision. The company filed no defence.

The DPA dismissed a cookie complaint regarding the absence of a “Reject all” button on the first layer of the cookie banner, as the “Confirm my choices” button meant that no cookies were placed since none of the categories of non-essential data were ticked by default.
The DPA dismissed a cookie complaint regarding the absence of a “withdraw consent” option as the controller set one up before the DPA’s investigation.

The DPA held that the publication of a former employee's photo in an online recruitment campaign by the former employer constitutes unlawful processing as it could not be based on consent, contract or legitimate interest.

The DPA held that a municipality’s unsolicited disclosure of the data subject’s identity to a property owner was unlawful. The data subject had reported the property owner for supposedly blocking a sidewalk to the municipality.

The DPA held that a controller cannot systematically request data subjects to submit a signed form and a copy of their ID for an access request, as facilitating the data subject's rights under the GDPR requires a case by case assessment.

The DPA found that a controller violated transparency principles by tracking geolocation data on a company vehicle outside of work hours and ordered the controller to bring its information disclosures into compliance with the GDPR.
The ICO issued an Enforcement Notice and 100,000 GBP fine against a controller due to unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals who were on the 'do not call' list.
The DPA reprimanded Bolt for failing to enable the rectification of a data subject’s phone number. However, the controller implemented the respective possibility in the course of the procedure.

The DPA held that a controller must give access to all the documents consulted when examining a data subject’s credit application, even if these documents were created by third entities for independent purposes

The DPA fined a controller that was processing employees’ fingerprint data € 360,000 because it failed to disclose processing and storage information to data subjects, lacked security measures ensuring the data’s confidentiality and failed to carry out a data protection impact assessment.

The Belgian DPA considered that regardless of the withdrawal of a complaint by a data subject, they still had the power to declare an infringement of the data subject's rights and issue a fine due to non-compliance with the GDPR.
The DPA found that a controller cannot be held liable for an action of an employee who deliberately disregarded the controller’s instructions.

The DPA fined a controller € 2.8 million for making personal data available in responses to all authentication attempts, including unsuccessful ones, and failing to prevent customer use of simple PINs.
The DPA fined a processor €800,000 for engaging a sub-processor without the prior authorization of the controller and for the belated notification of a data breach to the controller.

The DPA imposed a €300,000 fine against a medical technology firm for its use of the 'To' field instead of the 'Bcc' field when sending emails to the users of its app, leading to unauthorized processing of health data.

A complainant's health-related document (a refusal of travel and stay benefits for out-of-region treatment) was emailed by an administrative employee of the Sassari local health authority to a wrong third-party address. The authority also failed to answer the Garante's request for information until proceedings were opened. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5, 9 and 32 GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code. It fined the authority EUR 18,000, considering the severity low (one data subject, unintentional), and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased.

The press release (29 February 2024) announces the Garante's decision of 8 February 2024 fining Enel Energia over EUR 79 million for serious shortcomings in processing personal data for telemarketing. The case began with a Guardia di Finanza investigation, after which four other companies were fined and databases confiscated. Further checks showed Enel Energia had acquired 978 contracts from these companies, which were not part of its sales network, and that its customer-management and activation systems had security weaknesses that unauthorised agents exploited for years. At least 9,300 contracts were activated through these violations. A later note says the Court of Rome rejected the opposition and fully confirmed the decision, while a further appeal is pending.

The DPA fined an online gambling platform €2,000 after it failed to respond to an access request in time. It rejected the argument that access requests made for the purpose of gathering evidence for reimbursement claims were "manifestly unfounded".

An employee of a regional waste management agency complained that her 2019 evaluation form was registered in the agency's protocol system in a way visible to all authorised users, and that she had no contact with the data protection officer (DPO). The Garante found no unauthorised access, but found that the agency designated its DPO about three years late, did not publish the DPO's contact details, and did not notify them to the authority. Because these violations came from a single conduct, one fine of EUR 6,000 was imposed, with publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint and indicated that in the context of an erasure request, the controller was not expected to search of its own accord for the existence of data subject's email addresses other than the one mentioned by the data subject in the request.

The DPA dismissed a complaint regarding the potential theft of medical documents as well as suspicions relating to the failure to safeguard confidentiality and integrity due to the lack of evidence provided by the data subject.
The DPA fined a controller €5,000 and found that the failure to reply to an access request cannot be justified by general and vague circumstances, such as the COVID-19 pandemic emergency.
The Hellenic DPA decided the deletion of the data subject from the List of Inadmissible Third Country Nationals based on a special provision of the immigration legislation.

Energya VM Gestión de Energía, S.L., (“Energya VM” or “data controller”) entered into a contractual relationship with Nivalco, to promote its services. Nivalco contacted individuals from its database, offering discounts or insurance purportedly from their current energy supplier. However, these offers were actually agreements with Energya VM. Many data subjects only discovered they had entered into agreements with a new company when they noticed unexpected charges on their bank accounts. AEPD's investigation began following police reports of alleged crimes by energy supply companies. Energya VM failed to conduct a prior risk analysis analysis,ensure GDPR compliance in processing, and adopt measures for GDPR-compliant sales pitches. The AEPD found Energya VM negligent for allowing Nivalco’s deceptive practices to persist despite being aware of them at some point during the contractual relationship and imposed fines.
The Belgian DPA issued a warning against a controller for failing to provide clear information under Article 13 to the data subject.

The DPA fined a controller €3,500,000 after it failed to conduct an adequate risk assessment, overlooking avoidable security vulnerabilities that resulted in a data breach affecting 1,350,000 data subjects.

The DPA fined a company offering photography services at an amusement park €1000. The company took visitors' photos based on an implied consent which in reality could not be considered an affirmative action.
